title: Advertising and Saudi Media, 2000–2026: From Pan-Arab Satellite Television to Platform Economics: A Descriptive and Analytical Study
content: Advertising is the principal financial base of commercial media, and its scale, structure, and distribution shape what media institutions can produce. This study analyzes the role of advertising in the Saudi media industry across the 26-year period from 2000 to 2026, a span that opens with the consolidation of a pan-Arab satellite television market financed largely by Saudi capital and closes with a platform-dominated digital advertising economy operating under the Vision 2030 media strategy. Adopting a descriptive–analytical documentary design, the study triangulates industry expenditure estimates (Ipsos, IAB MENA, Statista), connectivity and audience data (DataReportal, the Communications, Space and Technology Commission), regulatory documents, corporate disclosures (MBC Group), and peer-reviewed scholarship to address three questions: how the scale, structure, and measurement of the Saudi advertising market have evolved; which conditions have sustained the advertising base of the media industry across the satellite and platform eras; and to what extent nine anticipated effects of advertising on the Saudi media industry, formulated at the dawn of the satellite era, have materialized. The findings show that Saudi Arabia became the largest national advertising market in the Middle East and North Africa, that digital media rose from under 10% of Gulf advertising expenditure in 2012 to roughly three-quarters of Saudi expenditure by 2023, and that an estimated 70–80% of digital spending flows to global platforms. Seven of the nine anticipated effects are supported or partially supported and two have been transformed: advertiser influence over content now operates through platform algorithms and influencer economies rather than through channel schedules, and advertising’s expected contribution to news credibility has been complicated by platform capture of revenue and by state ownership. The study concludes with recommendations on measurement, regulation, professionalization, and research.
